title: The Long Climb to the Clouds
script:
[hushed, reverent] The engine changes its note first. [break] A low, laboring growl, as the road tilts upward and the gearbox settles into the work ahead.

On either side, the maples burn. Scarlet, amber, a stubborn orange, all lit from behind by a low October sun. [soft tone] It is beautiful. [break] I hold on to that thought. I will need it.

[calm] This is Mount Washington, in New Hampshire. At six thousand, two hundred and eighty-eight feet, it is the highest peak in the northeastern United States, and it is famous for weather that turns in minutes. In 1934, an observatory on its summit recorded a wind of roughly two hundred and thirty-one miles an hour. The Auto Road has carried travellers toward that summit since the eighteen-sixties. It runs about seven and a half miles, and it climbs without apology, averaging around twelve percent, and touching far steeper.

[curious] At first, it is almost gentle. Birches flicker past. The tyres hum on warm tarmac. Somewhere behind my ears, a pulse begins, quiet and patient.

Then the trees start to shrink. [break] Spruce and fir, once tall and dark, crouch lower and lower, bent by winds that never rest. [nervous] Tree line arrives, and with it goes the last green wall between me and the view.

[anxious] And there is the valley. Vast, ridged, ablaze. Miles of crimson and gold folded into the distance like a quilt thrown over sleeping giants. I should be awestruck. Instead, I am watching the edge of the road.

[low and tense] The grade steepens. The engine strains. The brakes begin to smell warm. [break] The first hairpin comes. Wheel hard over. The bonnet points at the sky, then at nothing, then at the sky again.

[scared] Here, the barrier ends. [break] Or rather, it never really began. A low lip of stone, a few inches of loose gravel, and then, air.

My hands have gone pale on the wheel. [emphasis] Bone-white. My breath is shallow and quick. Don't look down. [break] I look down.

[long-break]

[awestruck] Hundreds of feet of autumn fall away beside my door, so lovely it feels almost cruel. The same gold that charmed me an hour ago now serves only to measure the distance.

[worried] Higher still, the mountain exhales. Cloud pours across the road and the valley is simply erased. A white wall, close enough to touch. The wind leans against the car like a hand on a door, and the steering turns light and strangely alive. Headlights on. The edge of the road is now only a rumor.

[whispering] Slow. Slow. Just the next bend. [break] And then the next.

[determined] Gravel crackles under the tyres, every stone distinct. My pulse hammers in my throat. The car crawls through the grey, and for a while the world is no larger than the few yards of road I can see in front of me.

Then, a gradual easing. The slope relaxes. The road widens, and levels, and a stone building looms out of the mist.

[long-break]

[sighing] The engine falls quiet. I set the handbrake and sit very still.

[relieved] My hands will not open at first. The fingers uncurl one by one, stiff, as if they had forgotten how. A laugh escapes me, shaky and absurd, and it is the best sound I have heard all day.

[awestruck] Then the cloud begins to tear. Slowly, a curtain drawn back, the sun finds the valley, and the whole country below me lights up. Ridge after ridge of fire, softened by distance, impossibly calm. From up here it is no longer a threat. It is simply a gift.

[moved] The mountain was never cruel. It was only indifferent, as mountains are, to our small machines and smaller courage. The fear was mine, and so, I think, is the memory.
